title: OPPI Data Hub Redesign
strategicSummary: Redesigned a complex government data hub to improve accessibility, usability, and navigation clarity for diverse public audiences.
responsibilities: Feedback sessions with stakeholders
Conducted user testing of site structure
Developed user flow maps
Created user flows for primary task scenarios
Documented requirements and acceptance criteria
Followed Brand and Style Guidelines
overview: The OPPI Data Hub serves as a central resource for public-sector data across multiple agencies. The existing site had grown organically over several years. This project focused on restructuring the navigation of the site and information architecture to create a clear, accessible, and intuitive experience.
problemAndGoals: The primary challenge was a disorganized content structure that made it difficult for users to locate relevant datasets and reports. Business goals included improving searching the site and achieving the task of saving data reports. Stakeholders needed a scalable architecture that could accommodate future navigation.
myRole: As a Technical Communication and Information Design professional, I took thorough notes and insightful responses from the stakeholder interview. I collaborated closely with another TCID professional to ensure the proposed architecture aligns with the style, branding, and existing workflows.
discoveryAndConstraints: Discovery included stakeholder interviews and feedback sessions, competitive analysis of 5 comparable data portals, and review of 'red-route' tasks usability testing. Key constraints included a fixed platform, a tight 3-month timeline, and the need to preserve all existing URLs for SEO continuity.
informationArchitecture: The new landing page IA reduced confusion, introduced a consistent tagging taxonomy for datasets, and established a clear hierarchy distinguishing raw data from interpretive reports. An interactive map with preset templates was implemented on the landing page for casual visitors.
userFlows: Three primary user flows were designed: finding and downloading a specific dataset, exploring trails, and accessing the latest published reports. Each flow was mapped from entry point through task completion, with decision nodes documented for edge cases and error states.
wireframesAndPrototypes: High-fidelity wireframes were created in Figma for all primary templates: homepage, category landing, dataset detail, and search results. A low-fidelity prototype was used in the stakeholder review session, with each round producing documented feedback and a revised iteration.
requirementsAndCriteria: Requirements were documented in Confluence, organized by user story. Each requirement included acceptance criteria written in Given/When/Then format. Accessibility requirements were integrated throughout rather than treated as a separate checklist, covering keyboard navigation, screen reader compatibility, and color contrast.
qaAndIteration: A thorough presentation of the heuristic evaluation of the prototype and stylistic branding visuals was given. Three iteration cycles addressed navigation labeling, filter behavior, and questions identified during presentation.
outcomesAndNextSteps: The redesigned architecture was approved and handed off to development with complete documentation. A structured competition for the changes was addressed in the site's About page.

title: Pikes Peak Library District Website Redesign
strategicSummary: IA and content strategy for a large public library system website, unifying 12 branch locations under a coherent, accessible digital experience.
responsibilities: Analyzed past site audit reports
Designed unified navigation architecture
Developed content templates and standards
Created accessibility requirements documentation
overview: Pikes Peak Library District operates 12 branch locations and serves a diverse community across El Paso County, Colorado. The digital translation of the platform needed to make information culturally and contextually relevant to a local community. This project unified the digital presence under a single, coherent information architecture.
problemAndGoals: The main objective was to create a mockup of the website, navigating resources for Spanish-speaking patrons studying for the naturalization exam or civics GED. The goal was to create one unified IA that served both casual visitors and frequent library users, reduced content maintenance burden for staff, and met WCAG 2.1 AA standards.
myRole: I created a content plan and outlined pages of materials providing localization. My deliverables included the content audit, new site map, content templates, and the accessibility requirements specification.
discoveryAndConstraints: Discovery included analyzing the Pikes Peak Library District website's branding, color scheme, typography, tone of voice, and information architecture. The primary constraint was working the pages within its templating system.
informationArchitecture: The new site map consolidated the pages to the hover menu, 'using the library's' services and resources. Each option created a simple and structured page with the information clearly labeled. Branch pages were standardized using a single template with locally editable zones.
userFlows: Key flows designed include creating personas that might use these resources differently. For example, a new immigrant might be studying for the citizenship tests, and another might be a high school student working on a  civics project.
wireframesAndPrototypes: Wireframes covered the page templates, from the homepage through event detail and digital resource landing pages. Prototypes were user tested with personas representing different digital literacy levels and accessibility needs.
requirementsAndCriteria: Content requirements specified writing standards, reading level targets for public-facing content, and structured data requirements for events. Technical requirements covered search indexing, language support, and site navigation.
qaAndIteration: The content skimmability was analyzed for heuristic and branding. Accessibility audit included automated scanning of all wireframes and manual review of interactive components for different user flow paths.
outcomesAndNextSteps: The new architecture reduced navigation items within reusable templates. A significant reduction in time required for user tasks, including direct translation for digital resources.

title: Colorado Springs Utilities Public Information Flyer
strategicSummary: Redesigned public utility communications to improve content clarity, plain language compliance, and accessibility for a diverse municipal audience.
responsibilities: Audited existing communications for clarity and accessibility
Applied plain language principles to technical content
Developed content hierarchy and layout recommendations
Created accessible design specifications
overview: Colorado Springs Utilities distributes public information materials to hundreds of thousands of customers across the Pikes Peak region. Many of these materials used technical language, dense formatting, and layouts that created barriers for residents. This project applied content strategy and plain language principles to improve communication effectiveness.
problemAndGoals: Confusion in the information already presented in the distributed materials, indicating comprehension failures rather than information gaps. Goals included improving first-read comprehension, reducing calls related to billing and service information, and ensuring materials met accessibility requirements.
myRole: As a Content Strategist, I analyzed the communications, identified content patterns that were confusing, and developed recommendations. I created the content in a flyer format, front and back, that could be left with mail or at residential areas.
discoveryAndConstraints: Discovery included identifying common confusion points and readability analysis. Constraints included brand guidelines that required significant negotiation to update, and printing specifications that limited layout flexibility.
informationArchitecture: Documents were restructured using a consistent hierarchy: key action or message first, supporting detail second, and reference information last. Recurring content blocks were identified and standardized across the materials to reduce inconsistency.
userFlows: Customer journeys were mapped for the three scenarios: understanding a higher-than-expected bill, setting up automatic payment, and reporting a service issue. Each journey identified the touchpoints where written materials played a role and where content gaps created friction.
wireframesAndPrototypes: Layout prototypes were developed for demonstrating improved visual hierarchy, white space, and typography. Each prototype included annotations explaining the content strategy rationale for key decisions.
requirementsAndCriteria: A content requirements document specified reading level targets, required accessibility metadata for digital versions, approved terminology for technical concepts, and review process requirements for future updates.
qaAndIteration: Materials were reviewed for accuracy. Two iteration cycles addressed terminology concerns from the technical reviewer and layout adjustments for print production.
outcomesAndNextSteps: Revised materials showed that the content style guide was extending the approach to digital communications and developing templates for routine notices.

title: Peak Vista Digital Style Video Templates
strategicSummary: Created a comprehensive digital style video template to standardize web communications across a multi-location community health organization.
role: Content Strategist & Social Media Content Creator
responsibilities: Analyzed voice, tone, and style guidelines
Created Video Templates
Maintained brand logo components
overview: Peak Vista Community Health Centers operates multiple locations serving underserved populations across southern Colorado. Their digital presence had grown without consistent standards, resulting in inconsistent voice, variable content quality, and patient-facing information that varied significantly across location pages. This project established a comprehensive digital style and content guide to unify their communications.
problemAndGoals: The goal was to create a practical, usable video template that non-specialist content contributors could apply without deep UX knowledge, while ensuring all content met accessibility and plain language standards.
myRole: The template can be used from initial audit through final publication and training. I collaborated with another technical communications and information design professional to ensure the guide addressed real workflows and integrated.
discoveryAndConstraints: Discovery included a content audit of web pages and analysis of related digital communications. A key constraint was that the guide needed to be maintained by non-technical staff, requiring clear governance processes and simple update procedures.
informationArchitecture: The guide was organized into five sections: Voice & Tone, Writing Standards, Page Templates, Component Standards, and Governance & Process. Each section was designed to be usable as a standalone reference, with cross-links to related guidance. A quick-reference card was created for the most common content tasks.
userFlows: The guide addressed three primary contributor workflows: creating a marketing video, event promotional content, and updating seasonal or time-sensitive content. Step-by-step process guides were developed for each workflow, integrated with the relevant standards sections.
wireframesAndPrototypes: Annotated page mockups were created showing correct application of content standards for each page template type. These served as both specification documents and training materials, illustrating the 'why' behind each standard.
requirementsAndCriteria: The template included branding, tone, iconography, typography, and style consistency check. Review and approval workflows were specified for content types with clinical or legal implications.
qaAndIteration: A pilot test was creating new content using only the template as a reference. Feedback was incorporated in two revision cycles, primarily improving the clarity of the page template section and adding more before/after writing examples.
outcomesAndNextSteps: The video template was developed with logos, social media handles, and iconography. Content contributors can have higher confidence in publishing decisions.

title: One Dog at a Time Colorado Audience Analysis & Content Strategy
strategicSummary: Conducted audience research and developed a content strategy to help a local animal rescue nonprofit better connect with adopters, volunteers, and donors.
responsibilities: Designed audience surveys
Developed audience personas and journey maps
Created content strategy recommendations
Conducted Content Audit
overview: One Dog at a Time Colorado is a small volunteer-run rescue organization placing dogs from rural shelters into local foster and adoptive homes. This project used audience research to identify the gaps between what the organization communicated and what their audiences needed to take action.
problemAndGoals: Web analytics on adoption non-profits showed high traffic but low conversion on key actions: adoption applications, foster sign-ups, and donation completions. The content audit addresses why interested visitors were not completing these actions and what content or structural changes would improve outcomes.
myRole: As a researcher and strategist on this project, the findings need to be synthesized to create realistic improvements. The findings include the research plan, administering all data collection, and developing the content strategy recommendations.
discoveryAndConstraints: Research included content audit of recent adopters, current fosters, and the organization's social media. The primary constraint was the organization's all-volunteer capacity—any recommendations made for only familiar engagement.
informationArchitecture: Analysis revealed that visitors were arriving primarily to see available dogs, but the path from browsing dogs to understanding the adoption process was unclear. The recommended IA changes included surfacing the adoption process earlier in the user journey, creating a dedicated foster page with a clear FAQ, and restructuring the donation page around impact stories rather than organizational needs.
userFlows: The user flows designed were the potential adopter journey (from dog browsing through application submission), the potential foster journey (from curiosity through first placement), and the donor journey (from interest through recurring giving setup). Each flow identified specific content needs at each step.
wireframesAndPrototypes: User flows were created for personas seeing social media posts and going to the adoption process page and the foster information page. These were presented  with content recommendations, not as final designs.
requirementsAndCriteria: Content recommendations were prioritized using an impact/effort matrix, allowing the team to sequence implementation realistically. Each recommendation included a content brief specifying the goal, audience, key messages, and success criteria.
qaAndIteration: Recommendations were reviewed and validated, based on the research findings from their own experience. One iteration cycle refined the social media picture first, recommendations based on the organization's foster intake process.
outcomesAndNextSteps: The content strategy was delivered as a prioritized roadmap with recommendations. The organization's implementation of a social media posts strategy would result in a measurable increase in foster applications.

title: Furniture Flipping App Concept
strategicSummary: Designed UX strategy and information architecture for a mobile app concept connecting furniture flippers with local buyers, focusing on trust, transaction clarity, and community.
responsibilities: Conducted competitive analysis of resale platforms
Developed app concept and value proposition
Designed information architecture and navigation model
Created user flows for core transaction scenarios
Built interactive prototype in Figma
overview: Furniture flipping—buying, refinishing, and reselling used furniture. This is a growing side economy with an active community of creators and buyers. Existing resale platforms were not designed for the unique needs of this niche: buyers want to see transformation stories, sellers need to communicate craft and quality, and transactions require local coordination. This concept project explored what a purpose-built platform for this community would look like.
problemAndGoals: Furniture flippers using general resale platforms reported frustration with low visibility for their work, difficulty communicating quality and provenance, and safety concerns around local meetups. The concept aimed to design an app that addressed these specific friction points while creating a community-centered transaction experience.
myRole: This was an independent concept project. I owned all phases from research through interactive prototype, treating it as a full UX strategy engagement to develop and demonstrate my process.
discoveryAndConstraints: Research included competitive analysis of 8 resale platforms (Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, OfferUp, Chairish, and others), interviews with a furniture flipper, and observation of online furniture flipping communities. The primary design constraint was mobile-first: the target audience managed all selling activity from their phones.
informationArchitecture: The app was organized around three core modes: Browse (discovery and shopping), Sell (listing creation and management), and Community (inspiration and connection). A persistent bottom navigation enabled quick switching between modes. Listing structure was designed to support transformation storytelling with before/after photos, materials documentation, and process notes.
userFlows: Primary flows designed: creating a listing with transformation story, discovering and purchasing a local item, scheduling a pickup meetup, and leaving a seller review. Safety features were integrated into the meetup flow, including location sharing and confirmation steps.
wireframesAndPrototypes: A complete interactive prototype was built in Figma covering the browse, listing, and transaction flows. The prototype included 40+ screens with realistic content and was tested with 4 participants from the furniture flipping community.
requirementsAndCriteria: A feature requirements document specified scope versus future phases, covering listing fields, transaction flow requirements, community features, and trust and safety requirements. Accessibility requirements were included, covering touch target sizing, color contrast, and screen reader support.
qaAndIteration: Prototype testing revealed that the listing creation flow was too long for mobile completion in a single session. The flow was redesigned to support saving drafts and resuming, and the step count was reduced from 7 to 4 by consolidating related fields. A second test round validated the revised flow.
outcomesAndNextSteps: The prototype was well-received, although feedback was to create a larger font. Next steps for the concept include a technical feasibility review, business model exploration, and a higher-fidelity prototype for investor presentation.

title: Nonprofit Grant Proposals
strategicSummary: Authored three targeted grant proposals for two nonprofits — a wildlife conservation group and a youth literacy program — securing funding through clear narrative structure, evidence-based impact statements, and funder-aligned language.
responsibilities: Conducted funder research and alignment analysis
Interviewed program staff to surface impact data
Drafted narrative sections: need statements, program descriptions, evaluation plans
Developed budgets and budget narratives
Revised proposals through multiple feedback cycles
Formatted final documents to each funder's submission guidelines
overview: This project encompassed three distinct grant proposals submitted on behalf of two nonprofits: Raptor Watch Colorado (a wildlife conservation organization) and Literacy Bridges (a youth reading intervention program). Each proposal required translating the organization's programs into funder-facing narratives that aligned with specific grant priorities, demonstrated measurable community impact, and complied with submission requirements.
problemAndGoals: Both organizations had compelling programs but struggled to communicate their impact in language that resonated with institutional funders. The primary challenge was bridging the gap between program-level knowledge — held by staff closest to the work — and the evidence-based, outcome-focused framing funders require. The goal for each proposal was to present a clear problem statement, a well-structured program design, and a credible evaluation plan within strict word and page limits.
myRole: I served as lead writer across all three proposals. For Raptor Watch Colorado, I wrote one federal-style proposal to a wildlife foundation and one community foundation proposal emphasizing local partnership. For Literacy Bridges, I wrote a corporate foundation proposal focused on literacy outcomes and ROI framing. I managed all drafts, incorporated feedback from program staff and an executive director, and formatted final submissions to each funder's specifications.
discoveryAndConstraints: Discovery involved intake interviews with program directors and a review of prior grant applications, annual reports, and program data. Key constraints included strict word limits (one proposal capped narrative sections at 1,000 words each), varying budget format requirements, and tight submission deadlines. I also had to ensure that program claims were grounded in documented data rather than anecdotal evidence to meet funder due-diligence standards.
informationArchitecture: Each proposal was structured around the standard grant narrative arc: organizational credibility, community need, program design, evaluation methodology, sustainability plan, and budget narrative. Within that arc, I tailored sequencing and emphasis based on each funder's stated priorities — for example, leading with ecological data for the wildlife funder and front-loading student outcome statistics for the corporate education funder.
requirementsAndCriteria: Requirements varied by funder. Federal-style guidelines required specific section headers and page counts. Foundation portals had character-limited text fields. All three proposals required signed assurances, organizational financials, and IRS determination letters. I created a compliance checklist for each proposal to track submission requirements and flag any missing elements before final review.
qaAndIteration: Each proposal underwent two to three revision cycles. First-draft reviews focused on clarity and narrative logic; second-round reviews incorporated program staff corrections to data and program descriptions; final reviews addressed funder-specific language, compliance items, and proofreading. I used a structured review template to ensure consistency across all three proposals.
outcomesAndNextSteps: All three proposals were submitted on time and to specification. The Raptor Watch Colorado community foundation proposal was funded in the first cycle. Literacy Bridges received a request for additional information from the corporate funder, which is an active part of the review process. Next steps include debriefing with both organizations on reviewer feedback and building a reusable grant narrative library to streamline future submissions.

title: Nonprofit Brand & Content Style Guide
strategicSummary: Developed a comprehensive brand and content style guide for a community arts nonprofit, establishing consistent voice, tone, and editorial standards across print, digital, and social channels.
responsibilities: Audited existing communications across all channels
Facilitated stakeholder workshops to define voice and tone
Documented grammar, punctuation, and usage standards
Created channel-specific writing guidelines
Built a terminology glossary and brand vocabulary list
Designed the guide layout for staff usability
overview: Mosaic Arts Collective is a mid-size community arts nonprofit serving underrepresented artists in southern Colorado. Over several years of growth, the organization's communications had become fragmented — varying voice across social media, grant materials, and event programs, and inconsistent terminology that confused patrons and funders alike. This project produced a living style guide that gave staff and volunteers a single authoritative reference for all written communications.
problemAndGoals: The organization lacked written standards for voice, tone, or grammar, which meant that each staff member applied their own interpretation to public-facing content. This created brand inconsistency, occasional accessibility failures (inconsistent alt-text practices, jargon-heavy language), and longer review cycles as leadership corrected variation before publication. The goal was a practical, usable guide that non-writers could apply confidently.
myRole: I led the project from discovery through final delivery. My responsibilities included running a two-session stakeholder workshop to define voice attributes, auditing 60+ communications samples across six channels, drafting all guide sections, and facilitating a staff pilot to test usability before final publication.
discoveryAndConstraints: The audit covered email newsletters, social media posts, grant narrative excerpts, event programs, website copy, and press releases from the prior two years. Key findings included 14 inconsistently used terms (e.g., 'patron' vs. 'audience member' vs. 'community member'), three distinct tonal registers with no established hierarchy, and no documented alt-text or plain language standards. The primary constraint was staff capacity — the guide needed to be scannable and actionable, not comprehensive in a way that discouraged use.
informationArchitecture: The guide was organized into six sections: Brand Voice & Tone, Writing for Specific Channels, Grammar & Mechanics, Accessible Writing Standards, Terminology Glossary, and Governance & Updates. Each section opened with a one-paragraph summary for quick orientation. A two-page Quick Reference Card extracted the highest-priority rules for staff who needed immediate guidance without reading the full document.
requirementsAndCriteria: Requirements were developed through stakeholder workshops and documented as a style decisions log, capturing not just the rule but the rationale behind each decision. Accessibility requirements were integrated throughout rather than siloed — plain language targets, alt-text standards, and color contrast guidance appeared in the sections where they were most relevant to the writer's context.
qaAndIteration: A pilot test asked four staff members to rewrite a sample email newsletter using only the guide as a reference. Pilot feedback drove two revision cycles: the channel-specific section was reorganized to lead with the most common task (social media posts), and the glossary was expanded with 11 additional terms surfaced during the pilot. A final accessibility review checked the guide document itself for readability and screen reader compatibility.
outcomesAndNextSteps: The guide was published as a shared Google Doc with version history enabled. Pilot participants reported higher confidence in publishing decisions and a reduction in revision requests from leadership. The governance section specifies a quarterly review cycle, with a named content owner responsible for updates. Next steps include adapting the guide for the organization's new volunteer onboarding program.

title: AI-Augmentation Workflow Report
strategicSummary: Researched and documented how AI writing and research tools can responsibly augment technical communication workflows, producing an internal report with adoption recommendations, risk analysis, and a practical usage framework.
responsibilities: Reviewed current AI writing and summarization tools
Tested tools against real technical writing task scenarios
Documented capability assessments and accuracy limitations
Developed a responsible-use framework
Wrote recommendations for phased adoption
Produced executive summary and full technical report
overview: As AI-assisted writing tools became increasingly available, technical communication teams faced a common challenge: understanding which tools provide genuine productivity value, which introduce accuracy or compliance risk, and how to establish guardrails that allow responsible adoption. This report was commissioned to evaluate three AI tools — ChatGPT, Claude, and Microsoft Copilot — against a defined set of technical writing task scenarios, and to produce adoption guidance grounded in documented evidence rather than vendor claims.
problemAndGoals: Organizations were making AI tool decisions based on marketing materials, individual staff experimentation, or both, with no systematic evaluation framework. The risk was either over-reliance on tools that hallucinate citations or omit regulatory language, or unnecessary restriction of tools that could genuinely reduce revision burden for lower-stakes content tasks. The goal was a structured capability assessment that supported an informed, tiered adoption decision.
myRole: I designed the evaluation methodology, executed all tool testing, documented findings, and wrote the full report including an executive summary and appendices. I also facilitated a review session with team leads to validate findings and pressure-test recommendations before final publication.
discoveryAndConstraints: Evaluation scenarios covered six technical writing task types: first-draft generation from structured notes, plain language revision of regulatory text, FAQ development from source documents, meeting summary generation, procedure step extraction, and citation checking. Each tool was tested against the same scenario set using identical inputs. Key constraints included the rapidly evolving nature of the tools (capability changes required documentation of tool versions tested) and the absence of an established external evaluation standard for this task domain.
informationArchitecture: The report was structured as: Executive Summary, Methodology, Per-Tool Capability Profiles, Cross-Tool Comparative Analysis, Risk Assessment (hallucination, confidentiality, attribution), Responsible-Use Framework, Tiered Adoption Recommendations, and Appendices (raw evaluation scoring rubric, test prompts and outputs). The executive summary was written to stand alone for leadership readers who would not review the full technical analysis.
requirementsAndCriteria: The evaluation rubric scored each tool on accuracy, task completion, tone appropriateness, citation handling, and editing burden reduction — rated on a four-point scale with documented evidence for each score. Responsible-use criteria were drawn from published technical communication ethics standards and adapted for AI-specific risks including fabrication and data privacy.
qaAndIteration: The draft report underwent review by two subject matter reviewers: a technical writing team lead and a data privacy officer. Their feedback produced a second iteration that strengthened the risk assessment section and added a data-handling decision tree for determining which content types could be processed through cloud-based AI tools under existing data governance policies.
outcomesAndNextSteps: The report was adopted as the internal AI usage policy foundation. The tiered adoption framework was incorporated into the team's onboarding documentation, and the responsible-use checklist became part of the content review process. Next steps include a six-month reassessment cycle to update capability profiles as the tools evolve.

title: UX Recommendation Report
strategicSummary: Translated UX research findings into a structured recommendation report for a municipal digital services team, providing evidence-based design guidance and a prioritized action roadmap.
responsibilities: Synthesized usability testing data and interview notes
Structured findings into actionable recommendation categories
Wrote evidence-backed rationale for each recommendation
Developed a prioritization matrix (impact vs. effort)
Created an executive summary for non-technical leadership
Formatted report to institutional documentation standards
overview: Following a round of usability testing and stakeholder interviews on a municipal permit application portal, the research team had rich qualitative and quantitative data but no structured deliverable to guide the design and development team. This report synthesized the research findings into a formal UX recommendation document — organized by severity, supported by evidence, and packaged for both design implementation and executive decision-making.
problemAndGoals: The research phase had produced session recordings, affinity diagrams, and a data spreadsheet, but the findings existed in fragmented form across multiple documents and team members. The design team needed a single, authoritative source they could hand to developers; leadership needed a high-level summary to approve resource allocation. The report had to serve both audiences without becoming so long that either group would skip it.
myRole: I was responsible for synthesizing the research data into the recommendation document. I worked directly with the UX researcher to validate my interpretation of findings, drafted all report sections, and iterated based on feedback from the design lead and a program manager who represented the leadership audience.
discoveryAndConstraints: Source materials included five usability session recordings (moderated think-aloud protocol), a post-session survey with 47 responses, a heuristic evaluation, and notes from three stakeholder interviews. Key constraints included a two-week delivery timeline and the need to communicate technical UX concepts to a mixed audience that included non-technical program staff and elected officials.
informationArchitecture: The report was organized into: Executive Summary, Research Overview and Methodology, Key Findings (grouped by theme, not session), Recommendations (severity-tiered: critical, important, enhancement), Prioritization Matrix, Implementation Notes, and Supporting Appendices (raw survey data summary, heuristic evaluation scores). Each recommendation followed a consistent structure: finding, evidence, recommendation, expected impact, and implementation complexity.
requirementsAndCriteria: Each recommendation required documented evidence linking it to a specific finding and, where available, a quantitative indicator (e.g., task completion rate, error frequency). Severity ratings followed a standardized scale defined in the methodology section. Implementation notes specified whether a change required development effort, content editing, or a configuration change — enabling the team to sort by their available capacity.
qaAndIteration: Two review cycles refined the report. The first addressed researcher feedback on finding interpretation accuracy. The second addressed program manager feedback on the executive summary — it was rewritten to open with resident impact rather than process description, and three recommendations were elevated based on stakeholder priority context that I had not captured in the initial synthesis.
outcomesAndNextSteps: The report was accepted as the primary handoff document for the portal redesign phase. The development team used the prioritization matrix to plan the first sprint. The executive summary was presented to the city's digital services committee and informed the approval of a supplemental UX budget for the next fiscal year.

title: SOP Template: Writing SOPs in Markdown and Exporting to PDF
strategicSummary: Designed and documented a repeatable SOP authoring system using Markdown as the source format and a CLI-based PDF export pipeline, reducing formatting overhead and enabling version-controlled procedure documentation.
responsibilities: Defined the Markdown-as-code documentation framework
Designed the SOP template structure and metadata schema
Built the Pandoc + CSS PDF export pipeline
Wrote the SOP-on-SOPs authoring guide
Created example SOPs demonstrating the template
Documented the Git version control workflow for procedures.
overview: Many teams write SOPs in Word or Google Docs, which creates version control challenges, inconsistent formatting, and high maintenance overhead when procedures change. This project developed a docs-as-code approach: SOPs are authored in Markdown, stored in a Git repository, and exported to consistently formatted PDF documents via a Pandoc build pipeline. The deliverable was both the system itself and the meta-SOP that teaches writers how to use it.
problemAndGoals: The problem is familiar in documentation-heavy teams: ten people maintaining SOPs in ten slightly different Word templates, no audit trail, no diff-based review, and PDFs that look different every time someone edits a header. The goal was a lightweight, open-source-based system that any writer could adopt without specialized tooling, that produced print-ready PDFs with consistent formatting, and that supported meaningful version history through standard Git workflows.
myRole: I designed the full system — the Markdown template schema, the Pandoc export configuration, the CSS stylesheet that controls PDF output, and the authoring guide (the SOP on making SOPs). I also wrote three example SOPs using the template to validate the system and demonstrate the range of procedure types it could support: a simple two-step checklist, a branching decision procedure, and a multi-role handoff process.
discoveryAndConstraints: Research included reviewing existing docs-as-code frameworks (Divio, Diataxis, GitBook conventions) and evaluating three PDF export tools: Pandoc, WeasyPrint, and a JavaScript-based solution. Pandoc was selected for its mature Markdown support, active maintenance, and ability to apply a custom CSS stylesheet for PDF output via wkhtmltopdf. Key constraints included keeping the authoring experience accessible to writers without a software engineering background — meaning no build-system complexity beyond a single terminal command.
informationArchitecture: The SOP template uses a YAML front matter block for metadata (title, version, owner, effective date, review date, approval chain) and a fixed Markdown section structure: Purpose, Scope, Definitions, Procedure Steps, Exceptions and Escalations, Related Documents, and Revision History. The authoring guide is itself written using the template, serving as both documentation and working example. The Git workflow section documents branching strategy, PR review requirements, and the automated PDF export trigger via GitHub Actions.
requirementsAndCriteria: The template was designed to meet common regulatory documentation standards including ISO 9001 procedure documentation requirements and FDA 21 CFR Part 11 audit trail considerations. Required metadata fields were defined as mandatory front matter keys; the export pipeline surfaces a validation error if required fields are missing. Accessibility requirements for the PDF output included heading structure, list formatting, and sufficient color contrast in the CSS stylesheet.
qaAndIteration: The system was tested by asking two writers with no prior Markdown experience to author a new SOP using only the authoring guide as a reference. Both writers successfully produced a correctly formatted PDF on the first attempt. Feedback drove two refinements: the Definitions section template was given more explicit placeholder guidance, and the Revision History table format was simplified to reduce entry friction.
outcomesAndNextSteps: The template system was published as an open repository with MIT license, including the full authoring guide, three example SOPs, and the Pandoc/CSS export configuration. The GitHub Actions workflow enables automatic PDF generation on any commit to the main branch. Next steps include adding a linter check for required front matter fields and developing a companion template for policy documents that share the same structural logic.

title: Translation Documents: Government & Literary Texts Using Cloud Services
strategicSummary: Produced two professional translations — a FEMA public preparedness document (English to Spanish) and a chapter from a contemporary novel (English to Spanish) — using cloud translation services augmented by post-editing, terminology management, and cultural adaptation.
responsibilities: Evaluated cloud translation service quality for each text type
Developed domain-specific terminology glossaries
Performed full post-editing on machine translation output
Applied plain language and cultural adaptation for government document
Maintained literary voice and stylistic register for the novel chapter
Documented the translation and post-editing workflow
overview: This project produced two completed translations using a cloud-assisted translation workflow: a FEMA public emergency preparedness guide (English to Spanish) intended for distribution to Spanish-speaking communities in Colorado, and Chapter 4 of a contemporary English-language novel (English to Spanish) as a literary translation exercise exploring the limits of machine translation for register and voice. Together, the two documents represent opposite ends of the translation spectrum — technical plainness versus literary expressiveness — and demonstrate how cloud translation services must be applied differently for each.
problemAndGoals: The government translation challenge was ensuring that FEMA's regulatory and procedural language was rendered in plain, accessible Spanish appropriate for readers with varying literacy levels — not a literal word-for-word transfer that preserved bureaucratic complexity. The literary translation challenge was the opposite: preserving idiomatic expression, narrative voice, and cultural resonance that machine translation systems consistently flatten. Both projects required documenting what cloud tools could and could not do reliably, producing a replicable post-editing workflow.
myRole: I served as translator and post-editor for both documents. discoveryAndConstraints: Source text evaluation preceded translation for both documents.
